subject: mathematics
question_text: If a = (b − c) sec θ, then prove that tan θ = (2√(bc)/(b−c)) sin(A/2).

mark_split.label: Expand and use the cosine rule

recall_prompt: Say how you would do this one — name each standard result you use and the order you use them in.

steps.label: Square the given relation
steps.margin_note: Two marks. sec and tan are the pair here, so the identity is sec²θ − tan²θ = 1 rather than the Pythagorean one.
lines: Given a = (b − c) sec θ ⇒ sec θ = a/(b − c)

recall.must_convey: That sec θ = a/(b−c) is squared and tan²θ = sec²θ − 1 formed.
accept: rearrange to sec theta then square and use tan squared equals sec squared minus one
the identity here is sec squared minus tan squared equals one
form tan squared from the given secant
sec theta square chesi minus one cheyyali
use the secant tangent identity

steps.why: sec and tan pair through sec² − tan² = 1, not through sin² + cos² = 1. Reaching for the wrong identity here is the commonest error in the family.
common_mistakes: Trying to convert to sines and cosines first.

steps.label: Expand and use the cosine rule
steps.margin_note: Two more marks. Note the ORDER: a² comes first now, so the bracket is 2bc MINUS the cosine-rule term, not plus.

recall.must_convey: That expanding (b−c)² gives 2bc − (b² + c² − a²), which becomes 2bc − 2bc cos A.
accept: expand b minus c squared and the bracket becomes two b c minus two b c cos A
the minus sign carries through so it is a subtraction this time
use the cosine rule with a minus in front
two b c minus two b c cos A vasthundi
expand and group with the minus

steps.why: Squaring (b − c) gives b² + c² − 2bc, so subtracting it flips both signs. Getting that right is what makes the next identity the sine one.
common_mistakes: Losing a sign and finishing with a cosine half angle.

steps.label: Introduce the half angle
steps.margin_note: Two more marks, and the point of difference. A MINUS in front of cos A means the SINE half-angle identity: 1 − cos A = 2sin²(A/2).

recall.must_convey: That 1 − cos A = 2sin²(A/2) is used, giving 4bc sin²(A/2)/(b−c)².
accept: one minus cos A is two sin squared half A so it becomes four b c sin squared half A
the minus means the sine half angle identity this time
use one minus cos A equals two sin squared half A
one minus cos A ante two sin square A by two
apply the sine half angle formula

steps.why: PLUS cos A gives a cosine half angle; MINUS cos A gives a sine one. That single rule tells you which of the two identities the answer needs, in every question of this family.
common_mistakes: Using the cosine half-angle form out of habit.
Missing that the sign changed from the twins.

steps.label: Take the square root
steps.margin_note: Last two marks. Same finish as the twins, but the answer carries sin(A/2) over b − c.

recall.must_convey: That the square root gives tan θ = (2√(bc)/(b−c)) sin(A/2).
accept: take the root to get two root bc over b minus c times sin half A
the answer has a sine and a b minus c
square rooting gives the required form
root teeste two root bc by b minus c into sin half A
the answer is two root bc over b minus c sin half A

steps.why: Every difference between this answer and its twins traces back to one minus sign in the question — the b − c, the sine, and the tan all follow from it.
common_mistakes: Writing cos(A/2) by copying the twins.
Writing b + c in the denominator.
